title: Monk Mollencup's pianist teaches him banjo chords
summary: A band pianist, annoyed by his wrong chords, draws him a map of the banjo and teaches him chords; Davison feels the banjo gives him no way to express himself.

bands.name: Monk Mollencup and His Society Orchestra

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: But, at that early age though, you could pick up songs just by hearing them once or twice, couldn't you?

Oh, yes. I always had a good ear for memorizing the lead to a song. The melody as it were. And, so, uh, all I did was strive to improve and I remember once -- this is running ahead of myself here, but-- once, being with a band and the piano player was very good; the band was a home town band called Monk Mollencup and His Society Orchestra and, occasionally, he'd have me and his band play the banjo. So, the piano player leaned over to me one night and said - "Why the hell don't you learn how to play the banjo?" Apparently, I was playing the wrong chords with the songs and - well, I said - "I'd like to. How the hell do you do that?" And, he said - "Well, I'll show you." So, he actually showed me the entire keyboard and what were minor chords and what were major chords and he showed me all that and he made a picture of the keyboard and what the little dots meant on the banjo, where you could slide up to that dot - would be

the right chord and he actually taught me how to play the banjo because he couldn't stand the way I played it. And, uh, it wasn't-- there wasn't any doubt that I was the worst one in the band, but I was determined to learn -- I really was. And, so, I used to play several jobs with him, but he mapped that thing out to me and I went home with that - that thing he wrote for me, you know, and I studied it. I really did, you know and I got to the point where I could read, as you know, all the music for a piano - had ukulele chords above and I got so I could read those ukulele cords just like anyone would read music. And, so, I liked that and I liked the banjo but I didn't--- it didn't seem to express my feeling. I was just another guy in the band playing rhythm and there was no way of expressing yourself on a banjo. You plunk away all night and I always thought I was the worst thing in the band. And, I wanted to do something else. So, I went to a lake one Summer--- we organized a small group in my home town and called ourselves - "The Ohio Lucky Seven"---
